# SK4032 — `Substring` is called to feed a search that takes a start index

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

`s.Substring(n).IndexOf(x)` copies the tail of the string onto the heap only to search inside it; `s.IndexOf(x, n)` reads the same characters in place.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Performance |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |
| Supersedes | S4635 |

## Why

`Substring` is an allocation and a copy proportional to what is left of the string, and the only thing done with the result here is a search that already accepts the offset as an argument. `IndexOf(value, startIndex)` and `IndexOfAny(anyOf, startIndex)` begin exactly where the copy would have begun and never build it. `SK1028` makes the span-based version of the same argument; this one needs no new type at the call site at all, which is why it is the first thing to reach for.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (path.Substring(prefix.Length).IndexOf('/') >= 0) {
    Split(path);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
if (path.IndexOf('/', prefix.Length) >= 0) {
    Split(path);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The two expressions do not return the same number, and everything about this rule follows from that.** `s.Substring(n).IndexOf(x)` is an index into the copy; `s.IndexOf(x, n)` is an index into `s`; they differ by exactly `n`. So the finding is raised only where the result is used as a *presence test* — compared with `0` or `-1` by `>= 0`, `< 0`, `> -1`, `<= -1`, `== -1` or `!= -1`, in either operand order — because that is the one question both spellings answer identically. Where the number is assigned, returned, passed on, or compared with anything else, the rule is silent; a fix there would have been a silently wrong offset, which is worse than the allocation. ⚠ **`LastIndexOf` is excluded rather than overlooked**: its `startIndex` overload searches *backwards* from that position, so the substitution is not a narrower search but the opposite one. ⚠ Only the one-argument `Substring(n)` qualifies — `Substring(n, length)` bounds the search as well as moving its start, and the rewritten call would look past the end of what was asked for. ⚠ The start-index overload is looked up on the compilation's own `string` rather than assumed: `IndexOf(char, StringComparison)` exists and `IndexOf(char, int, StringComparison)` does not, so a rule that appended an `int` to whatever overload it saw would write a call that does not bind. ⚠ The offset and every search argument must be a literal or a path of names. Moving the offset after the arguments changes the evaluation order, and rather than reason about whose side effects could see whose, the rule declines when either side could have any. ⚠ The boundary cases were checked and agree: at `n == s.Length` both spellings answer "not found"; for an empty search string both answer "found" (at different positions, which is why only the presence test is offered); and both throw `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` for the same out-of-range `n`. ⚠ `s.Substring(n).Contains(x)` is deliberately out of scope, because its rewrite turns a `bool` atom into a relational expression and that needs the surrounding-syntax analysis `SK1034` does for `Any()`.
